standard.title: Migration and changing nations
standard.description: reasons for, and effects of, internal migration and international migration in Australia, China or other countries
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain factors that influence where people live (AC9HG7K05) and cultural connectedness to places (AC9HG7K07). They have not yet examined migration as a driver of population change at national or international scales.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the reasons for and effects of internal and international migration in Australia, China or other countries, including the relationship between migration and urban concentration.

nodes.label: Types and patterns of migration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the main types and patterns of internal and international migration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify and explain at least two types of migration (e.g., permanent, temporary, forced) with an example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the main types and patterns of migration — permanent migration, temporary labour migration, student migration, forced migration (refugees, illegal migrants, trafficked people) and circular migration — and distinguish internal from international migration.
wider: Examine how legal status shapes the experience and rights of different migrant categories.
Compare the relative scale of voluntary vs forced migration globally and how these ratios change over time.
Investigate how the concept of 'circular migration' challenges traditional models of permanent settlement.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear typology of migration types, students conflate voluntary and forced migration, permanent and circular, and produce confused explanations of causes and effects. The typology is the analytic foundation for Nodes 2 and 3.

response_modes.reason: The typology of migration requires explicit definitional work. A classification framework distinguishing voluntary/forced and permanent/temporary prevents undifferentiated 'people move for jobs' explanations.

success_criteria: Identifies and explains at least three migration types (e.g., permanent, forced, circular) with a located example of each.
Distinguishes internal migration from international migration.

nodes.label: Reasons for migration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the reasons — economic, social, political and environmental — driving internal and international migration in Australia, China or other countries.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least two reasons for migration with examples from a named country.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain multiple drivers of migration — mining developments and employment (Australia: Pilbara, Bowen Basin), chain migration linked to family and employment, changing economic conditions, cultural events and circular mobility — across Australia and/or China.
wider: Compare the relative weighting of economic vs social vs political drivers in different migration flows.
Examine how climate-driven displacement is reshaping traditional migration patterns.
Investigate how the reasons for migration have changed over time — comparing 1950s migration to present-day patterns.

response_modes.reason: Using multiple migration examples across Australia and China — rather than a single case study — prevents students from treating one migration context as the universal pattern.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of migration drivers — economic, cultural, family network, political — and the contrast between Australia and China as case studies offer rich comparative geographic reasoning. Wider students can develop nuanced, multi-causal migration explanations.
success_criteria: Explains at least two reasons driving a specific migration flow in a named country.
Connects the migration reasons to the type of migration (internal/international, permanent/temporary).

nodes.label: Effects of migration on places
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of internal and international migration on places of origin and destination, including the relationship between migration and urban concentration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain one effect of migration on a place of origin or destination.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the effects of migration on places of origin and destination — population growth in mining regions, cultural diversity in cities, urban concentration patterns — and interpret population data to describe the relationship between international migration and urban concentration in Australia, and internal migration and urban concentration in China.
wider: Examine the brain drain effect — how migration of skilled workers affects places of origin.
Investigate how migrant communities reshape the cultural character of destination places (language, cuisine, religious infrastructure).
Compare how the effects of internal migration in China differ from international migration into Australia, considering scale and policy context.

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together migration typology, reasons and spatial patterns into an explanation of effects on places — including using population data as evidence for the migration-urbanisation relationship.

success_criteria: Explains at least two effects of migration on a named place of origin or destination.
Interprets population data to describe the relationship between migration and urban concentration in at least one country.
